summary:
ASTRA is a free phone game where children aged 7 to 12 run a Moon base near the lunar South Pole. Players pick one of NASA's nine candidate landing regions, lead a crew of four (power, air, plants, radio), and share the few power blocks the sunlight gives each day. Every day brings a new problem, moonwalks earn science, and the mission is won when the science goal is reached.

The data is real. Each region's sunlight and Earth view come from NASA LRO LOLA maps. Solar flares come from NASA's DONKI records: players read a flare's clues, decide whether to power the shield, then see in NOAA GOES data whether a proton storm followed. Of 424 big flares from 2011 to 2026, only 98 brought one within 72 hours, so kids learn that a big flash does not always mean danger.

Most space lessons give children facts. ASTRA gives them hard choices: every block spent on one system is missing from another. It works offline after the first visit, has no ads or accounts, and includes a page for teachers, so any school with a phone can use it. Next, we plan a Bangla version and classroom trials.
details:
What it does

ASTRA is a free phone game for children aged 7 to 12. The player runs a Moon base near the lunar South Pole for 10 days (Cadet) or 20 days (Commander).

1. Pick a place. The map shows NASA's nine candidate landing regions. Each one has its own share of sunlight (power) and of time with Earth in view (radio), taken from NASA LRO LOLA maps.

2. Share power. Sunlight gives only a few power blocks a day. The child drags them to air, plants, radio or the radiation shield, and every block spent on one is missing from another. Four crew members show the jobs: power, air, plants and radio to Earth.

3. Read the Sun. A real solar flare from NASA's DONKI records arrives with clues: its size, whether it threw a gas cloud, and (in Commander) which side of the Sun it came from. The child guesses whether space rays will follow and decides whether to charge the shield.

4. See what happened. The next day the game shows what the Sun did, using the NOAA GOES proton record. Then come the day's surprise problem, a moonwalk to earn science, and the next decision. The mission is won when the science goal is reached.

Mission Control answers after the real Earth-Moon radio delay of 1.28 seconds. In Commander mode the radio is down whenever Earth is out of view, matching the chosen region's LOLA data.

Benefits and intended impact

Most space lessons give children facts. ASTRA gives them decisions with costs, and it lets them check their guesses against real history. Of 424 big flares (class M5 and above, 2011 to 2026), only 98 were followed by a proton storm within 72 hours, so kids find out for themselves that a big flash does not always mean danger. They practise planning ahead, sharing a scarce resource and reading evidence before acting.

We tested whether the clues teach something with computer test players, 360 Cadet games each. Players who read the clues won 86.7% of games, players who ignored them won 51.9%, and random tapping won 7.5%.

ASTRA is free, works offline after the first visit, needs no account and shows no ads, so a school in Bangladesh with one shared phone can use it. A page for teachers explains the science and the data. Next, we plan a Bangla version and classroom trials.

How it is creative

The game never invents an outcome. Every flare is a real event, and the "You said / The Sun did" moment turns a NASA archive into a guessing game a child wants to win. Each mission mixes flares that brought rays with flares that did not, so there is a pattern to learn, while the game says plainly that in real life most flares bring no rays.

Tools and languages

TypeScript and React 19, built with Vite and installed as a PWA (vite-plugin-pwa) so it runs offline. Vitest for unit tests and the test players, Playwright for phone-size (360 x 740) tests and offline play, and axe-core for an accessibility scan of every child screen. A Node script (scripts/ingest.mjs) pulls and counts the NASA data. Hosted on GitHub Pages; code under Apache-2.0. Crew art: Open Peeps (CC0). Icons: Lucide. Font: Nunito.

Factors we considered

-Young players: picture-first screens with about 12 visible words at most, big touch targets, a picture for every sound, a Calm mode with no motion, and read-aloud with the device's own voice.

-Honest data: outcomes are NASA records. Storm sizes for 90 of the 98 followed flares are simplified, and the game says so on screen. Today's Sun is labelled LIVE, SAVED or FROM THE PAST, and test data is never shown as live. The landing regions are presented as candidates, not a landing plan.

-Safety and privacy: no accounts, no ads, no real children's names, faces or voices, and no NASA logo. ASTRA uses NASA data and is not made or endorsed by NASA.

-Schools with few devices: offline play after one visit, on any phone with a web browser.

AI use: Claude (Anthropic) helped write the code and text, and helped build the demo video. The video narrator is Kokoro-82M, a stock voice run locally. The video carries an "AI voice · AI-assisted edit" tag, and the game's About and Data pages state that Claude helped make it.
